text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
Great German composer LUDWIG VAN BEETHOVEN was born in 1770. English novelist JANE AUSTEN, whose major works include "EMMA" and "Pride and Prejudice", was born in 1775.
Australian composer ALFRED HILL was born in 1870. He wrote "Waiata Poi" and became a world-wide success with the recording by PETER DAWSON.
One of the most significant forces in English theatre NOEL COWARD was born in 1899. His best-known plays include "Hay Fever" and "Blithe Spirit". He became Sir NOEL.

American anthropologist MARGARET MEAD was born in 1901. She studied the Samoans and Trobriand Islanders and created great interest in their supposed sexual habits. British science-fiction writer ARTHUR C. CLARKE was born in 1917. His fictional ideas inspired modern space research. Norwegian actress LIV ULLMAN, who appeared in INGMAR BERGMAN films, was born in 1939.

'ABBA' group member BENNY ANDERSON was born in 1946. The Swedish pianist, singer and songwriter came to prominence as a member of the group 'Hep Stars' in the sixties in Sweden. In 1970 BENNY and BJORN ULVAEUS joined up and with their wives started the hugely successful 'ABBA'. They released their first album in 1972 under the name of 'BJORN, BENNY, AGNETHA and ANNI-FRID'. They used their initials to create the name 'ABBA'. Hits included "Waterloo"(1974), "Fernando"(1976), "Dancing Queen"(1976), and "Take A Chance On Me"(1978).

US guitarist and singer/songwriter with 'ZZTop' BILLY GIBBONS was born in 1949. Prior to forming the group he played in supporting bands for JIMI H*NDRIX, who said GIBBONS was one of the best young guitarists in the States. In 1970 the first album by 'ZZTop' appeared. Their hits included "Tush"(1975), "Legs"(1984), "Gimme All Your Lovin'"(1983), "Stages"(1986) and "Rough Boy"(1986).
** EVENTS **
1773 : The "Boston Tea Party" show American colonists

attack three ships in Boston Harbour in their campaign against British control. Disguised as Indians the protestors boarded the ships and emptied 342 chests of tea worth 16,500 dollars into the sea. The action was in protest to the tea tax imposed on the colonies to rescue the East India Company from bankruptcy. The tea tax was a hang-over from the 1765 Stamp Act which imposed new taxes on the colonies to help pay for the costs of the Seven Years' War. The taxes met with boycotts and violent rejection. They were replaced by the Townsh*nd Acts' new taxes on tea, lead, glass, paper and paint. This act was also repealed after organised opposition. The tea tax was the last remaining tax.
1809 : NAPOLEON divorced his beloved JOSEPHINE because
she was not able to provide him with an heir.
1850 : The first immigrant ship the "CHARLOTTE JANE" arrived
in New Zealand.
1929 : One miner was shot dead and nine others wounded

when police fired on rioting coal miners at Rothbury in New South Wales. Seven police were also injured as they tried to break up the demonstration. Eight thousand miners converged on Rothbury in response to the state government's plan to use voluntary workers to break the ten-month long dispute which had closed New South Wales' mines.The strike was caused by a proposal for miners to accept lower wages or to allow non-union labour to work the mines. Three days after the riot the federal Arbitration Court handed down an interim award restoring the higher wages. A month later the High Court found in favour of the mine owners saying the interim award was invalid. In June 1930 the miners returned to work with a restoration of conditions that existed before the stoppage.
1949 : A quarter of a million white Afrikaners att*nded

the opening of the Voortrekker monument in Pretoria. The monument was opened on a religious holiday - the annual day of thanksgiving for God granting battle victories. These victories were the 1838 defeat of the Zulus and the 1880 defeat of the British. Divine protection however did not ext*nd to the Boer War. In 1948 the right-wing Afrikaner National Party won the South African elections and the Boers thanked God for that victory as well.
1969 : Six people were killed in Calcutta when 20,000
fans stampeded for tickets on the last day of the fourth Test, which Australia won by 10 wickets.
1969 : Australia's Prime Minister Mr GORTON annouced that

there would be a phased withdrawal of Australian troops from Vietnam to coincide with the next "substantial" withdrawal by Americans. GORTON's announcement came hot on the heels of US President NIXON announcing that a further 50,000 troops would go home.
1979 : One of the world's rarest mammals, the Queensland

hairy-nosed wombat, was said to be on the verge of extinction. The state's wildlife department said there were fewer than 40 left and the department would be working towards fencing off the wombats' living area.
1988 : Britain's junior health minister EDWINA CURRIE

resigned with "egg on her face". She announced that most British eggs were infected with salmonella. This brought angry demands for compensation from farmers as egg prices plummetted. Eggs were implicated in a series of food poisoning scares and organic farmers claimed there was no way to ensure chickens were healthy in overcrowded battery hen farms.
1990 : Forty-five year old Scottish rocker ROD STEWART
married 22-year-old model RACHEL HUNTER.
1991 : In London, the new director-general of the
security service M15 was officially named for the first time. It was STELLA RIMINGTON, the first-ever female boss of the agency.
